note.explanation: A hypothesis that is supported by experiments can lead to a theory. Scientists continue to test theories, and a theory proved repeatedly by experiments becomes a law or principle.
examples: The theory of evolution explains how species change over time through natural selection.
Hardy-Weinberg law and Mendel’s laws of inheritance are examples of biological laws.
note.checkAnswer: Experiments support hypotheses; repeated testing can lead to a theory and then a law or principle.
note.simple: Test an idea, test it again, and use the results to build scientific explanations.
note.checkQuestion: According to your textbook, what can a theory become if experiments prove it again and again?
note.title: From Hypothesis to Theory and Law
steps: Scientists use the supported hypothesis to make further hypotheses.
When the new hypotheses are also proved, the original hypothesis becomes a theory.
Scientists keep testing the theory and try to disprove it.
If experiments prove it again and again, it becomes a law or principle.
note.answer: A theory that is proved again and again by experiments becomes a law or principle.

written.text: How a hypothesis is converted to theory, law and principle?
written.finalAnswer: Experiments prove a hypothesis correct; scientists use it to make further hypotheses. When these are also proved, the original hypothesis becomes a theory. A theory is supported by extensive evidence and repeatedly validated by multiple researchers. Scientists continue testing it and try to disprove it. If it is proved again and again by experiments, it becomes a law or principle, a uniform or constant fact of nature.

written.text: What are the basic steps a scientist adopts in order to solve a scientific problem?
written.finalAnswer: A scientist studies a biological problem, makes observations, proposes hypotheses, draws deductions, and tests them through experiments using experimental and control groups. The scientist records the results and reports them. If a hypothesis is proved, it may provide a solution and, after further testing, contribute to a theory or law.

written.text: How can a scientist apply the scientific method to confirm an observation that a certain plant species grows more quickly in shady places than in direct sunlight?
written.finalAnswer: The scientist should observe and record the plant’s growth in shady places and in direct sunlight, propose a hypothesis, and make a deduction about the expected growth. The scientist should test it with controlled experiments using comparable plants, keeping other conditions the same and varying the light exposure. The results should be recorded, compared and reported. Repeated results can support the hypothesis, while results that do not agree may disprove it.

rubric.why: The observation must be considered in both light conditions being compared.
rubric.how: State that plant growth in shade and direct sunlight will be observed or compared.

rubric.why: A hypothesis gives a testable explanation or prediction for the observation.
rubric.how: State a hypothesis about faster growth in shade.

rubric.why: A fair test requires experiments that control other conditions while comparing light exposure.
rubric.how: Compare similar plants, vary light exposure and keep other conditions the same.

rubric.why: Recorded experimental results are used to evaluate the hypothesis.
rubric.description: Explain how the hypothesis is evaluated.
rubric.how: State that results are recorded and compared to see whether they support or disprove the hypothesis.

modelAnswer: Observe and record the growth of the plant species in shady places and in direct sunlight.
Propose the hypothesis that the plants grow more quickly in shade and make a deduction about the expected results.
Test the hypothesis in controlled experiments using comparable plants; keep other conditions the same and vary the light exposure.
Record and compare the results, then report them.
Repeated results may support the hypothesis; results that do not agree may disprove it.

explain.title: How a hypothesis becomes a theory
explain.body: Experiments can prove a hypothesis correct. Scientists then use it to make further hypotheses. When those are proved too, the original hypothesis becomes a theory. A theory has extensive evidence and is repeatedly validated by multiple researchers.

explain.title: Why theories are tested again
explain.body: Scientists keep testing theories and try their best to disprove them. This helps them check whether the theory continues to fit the evidence.

explain.title: What a scientific law is
explain.body: The textbook defines a scientific law as “a uniform or constant fact of nature.” In this section’s sequence, a theory proved again and again by experiments becomes a law or principle. Hardy-Weinberg law and Mendel’s laws of inheritance are examples.

explain.title: The scientific-method flowchart
explain.body: Figure 1.4 shows a sequence from a biological problem to observations, hypotheses, deductions, experiments, results and reporting. Experiments include experimental and control groups. Further testing can lead to a theory or solution and then a law or principle.

mistakes: Do not say a hypothesis becomes a theory after only one experiment; include further hypotheses being proved.
Do not leave out extensive evidence and repeated validation when describing a theory.
Do not say scientists stop testing a theory; the section says they keep testing it and try to disprove it.
Do not confuse a theory with a law: state that a law is a uniform or constant fact of nature.
When writing the scientific-method sequence, do not place deductions after experiments; the flowchart places deductions before experiments.
